paragraphs.text: Snow that falls on a high polar plateau does not melt. It is buried by the snow of the following year, compressed by the weight above it, and turned into ice that preserves, in order, the air that was trapped between the flakes. A column drilled from such a place is therefore a sequence of samples of the atmosphere, and the deepest of them reach back through several complete cycles of ice ages. Nothing else on earth records the composition of the air directly rather than by inference.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Drilling one is a slow industrial operation carried out in a place with no roads. A deep hole takes several seasons, requires a fluid to keep it from closing under pressure, and produces cores in sections that must be logged, packed and kept below minus twenty degrees from the moment they leave the barrel until they reach a laboratory on another continent. A single break in that chain destroys the gas record in the affected section, and the logistics of the cold are a larger part of the budget than the drilling.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Dating the layers is the discipline behind everything else. In the upper part of a core the annual layers can be counted directly, as summer and winter snow differ in the size of their crystals and in chemistry; deeper down the layers thin under pressure until counting fails, and the age is then modelled from the flow of the ice and checked against known markers. Volcanic eruptions leave a spike of sulphate in ice around the world within a year or two, which ties cores from both hemispheres to each other and to historical records.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The air bubbles are the famous part of the record and carry an awkward complication. Snow remains porous for decades after it falls, so the air trapped at a given depth is younger than the ice around it, sometimes by centuries, and the difference varies with temperature and accumulation. Comparing a gas measurement with a temperature measurement from the same depth therefore requires correcting for that gap, and much of the argument about what the cores show has been an argument about the correction rather than about the measurements.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Temperature itself is not measured but inferred. Water molecules containing heavier isotopes of oxygen and hydrogen evaporate slightly less readily and condense slightly more readily, so the isotopic composition of snow depends on the temperature at which it formed. The relationship is calibrated against modern observations and against boreholes in which the residual heat of past climates can still be detected, and the result is a temperature curve with error bars that widen the further back it goes.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: What the cores established is the thing everybody now quotes. Carbon dioxide and methane rise and fall with temperature through every glacial cycle, and the pre-industrial range of carbon dioxide stayed within a band that the present value passed several decades ago. The cores do not by themselves prove what causes what within a cycle, and specialists are careful about that; what they do show is the size of the band and how far outside it the present composition sits.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The oldest ice is the current prize. Continuous records extend back around eight hundred thousand years, and the periodicity of ice ages changed about a million years ago for reasons that are not settled; recovering ice from before that change would test the competing explanations directly. Several teams are drilling in places where old ice may survive near the bed, and the difficulty is that ice near the bed is deformed, melted from below, or mixed, so a core may be old and useless at the same time.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The archive is also disappearing in the places that are easiest to reach. Mountain glaciers hold records of regional climate and of pollution, and many of them now melt at the surface each summer, which moves meltwater down through the layers and erases the sequence. Several projects are drilling such glaciers not to study them now but to store the cores, on the reasoning that questions will be asked in fifty years of material that will not exist by then, which is an unusual argument to have to make to a funding committee.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: The horse that changed the steppe

paragraphs.text: The horse was domesticated late and mattered more than almost anything domesticated before it. Cattle, sheep and goats were kept for thousands of years first, and they changed what people ate; the horse changed how far and how fast they could move, which changed everything else. The evidence for when and where this happened has been rewritten twice in thirty years, first by a new way of reading teeth and then by the ability to sequence ancient genomes, and the current account is firmer than either of the two it replaced. It is also a good illustration of how a field decides that something is known.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Bones are a poor guide on their own. A wild horse and a horse kept for meat leave similar remains, and the change in body shape that follows domestication takes centuries to appear, so an archaeologist looking at a pile of bones cannot easily say whether the animals were hunted or herded. The proportion of young males in a deposit is suggestive, because herders cull them and hunters take what they find, but it is a statistical argument about a small sample and it has been read both ways. The same deposit has appeared in one paper as evidence of herding and in another as evidence of a successful hunt.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Teeth turned out to carry a clearer signal. A bit held in a horse’s mouth rubs against the second premolar and leaves wear that does not occur naturally, and the wear survives on archaeological teeth. Finding it means the animal was ridden or driven rather than merely eaten, which is the question that matters. The method has limits: a soft bit of rope or sinew leaves less wear than a metal one, and the absence of wear therefore proves nothing. Where the wear is present, however, it is difficult to explain any other way, which makes it a one-sided test worth having.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Ancient DNA changed the picture again and in an unexpected direction. Sequencing horses from across Eurasia showed that the population which became every modern domestic horse spread rapidly from a single region a little over four thousand years ago, replacing other horse populations almost everywhere within a few centuries. Earlier candidates for the first domestic horses turned out to belong to lineages that left few descendants, which means there were probably several attempts and one of them succeeded overwhelmingly.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: What the successful lineage carried has been identified in part. Two genetic changes distinguish it, one associated with a calmer response to stress and one affecting the strength of the back, and both would matter a great deal to anybody trying to ride an animal for a day. It is tempting to say that these were selected deliberately; it is safer to say that animals with them were easier to keep and to breed, and that the selection was probably an outcome rather than a plan.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The consequences are visible in the archaeology within a few generations. Settlements spread into grassland that could not support farming, goods moved along routes that had carried nothing before, and languages spread in patterns that follow the same directions, which is why the horse appears in arguments about linguistics that have nothing to do with animals. Warfare changed too, though later than the popular account suggests: the chariot came first and the effective mounted warrior is a development of the following millennium.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The horse also reshaped the landscape it moved through. Large herds grazed grassland in a way that maintained it against scrub, and the routes they made became the routes that later carried carts, then roads. In several regions the oldest surviving lines on the map are tracks that make sense only if the traveller is on a horse, keeping to the high dry ground and avoiding the wet valleys that a modern road follows. The pattern is easier to see from the air than from the ground.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the case shows about method is as interesting as what it shows about horses. Each of the three lines of evidence — bones, teeth, genomes — was in its turn described as decisive and each was later qualified, and the account that now stands is the one supported by all three rather than by the newest. Fields that reach a conclusion by one method tend to revise it when a second arrives; fields that wait for agreement between methods move more slowly and turn around less often.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Should the state pay for the orchestra?

paragraphs.text: Almost every country with a symphony orchestra pays for it out of public money, and almost every country argues about whether it should. The argument is old enough that both sides have worn grooves: one describes a public good that the market cannot supply, the other a subsidy paid by many for the pleasure of a few. The interesting material is in between, in what the audience figures, the accounts and the outreach programmes actually show.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Clara Mensah begins with the economics of the form. A symphony orchestra has needed roughly the same number of players for two centuries, so it cannot increase output per worker the way a factory can, while its musicians must be paid enough to keep them from other work whose productivity does rise. Costs therefore climb faster than prices in the rest of the economy, and a ticket that covered the cost in 1900 cannot do so now. This is not mismanagement, she argues, but arithmetic that applies to every live performance.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Anders Holm accepts the arithmetic and questions who pays and who benefits. Surveys of concert audiences in several countries find them older, wealthier and better educated than the population that funds them through taxation, and he regards the gap as the central fact rather than an embarrassing detail. Subsidy that flows to institutions attended by the comfortable is, in his description, a transfer upwards, and it is defended in language — heritage, civilisation, the national repertoire — that makes the transfer hard to discuss in ordinary terms.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Beatriz Salas answers that the audience in the hall is the wrong measure. Her orchestras play in schools and hospitals, record for broadcast, lend instruments and run ensembles for children in districts with no music teaching, and the audience for all of that is nothing like the audience for a Thursday concert. She accepts that some of this work is decorative, added to a funding application and abandoned when the grant is signed; she argues that the answer is to fund the work properly and audit it, not to use its weakest examples as an argument against the whole.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Viktor Lang is interested in what subsidy does to the art. An institution that depends on an annual grant becomes careful, he argues, and careful institutions programme the familiar, because an empty hall in a subsidised season is a political problem rather than a commercial one. He points to the contrast with ensembles that survive on project funding and tour, which take more risks and disappear more often. His conclusion is not that subsidy is bad but that permanent subsidy without a requirement to take risks produces a museum with a payroll.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The evidence on the economic case that cities usually make is not encouraging. Studies of cultural institutions as drivers of local economies find effects that are real, small and mostly transfers from other local spending; the visitor who buys a concert ticket frequently buys one fewer restaurant meal. The honest version of the economic argument is narrower: a hall keeps a city centre occupied on a winter evening, and that has a value which is not captured by counting tickets.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What has changed the practical argument is the collapse in the cost of listening. Every recording ever made is available for the price of a coffee a month, which removes the old justification that subsidy preserves access to the repertoire, and increases the value of the thing recordings cannot supply, which is a hall full of people hearing the same sound at the same time. Orchestras that have understood this sell the occasion and the place; those that have not still describe themselves in the language of the record catalogue.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The defensible position is a narrow one and requires work rather than assertion. Public money for an orchestra is justified if the institution is genuinely open, if the education work is real and inspected, if the programming risks something, and if the accounts are published in a form a councillor can read. Institutions that meet those conditions are worth the money by the ordinary standards applied to a library or a park. Institutions that do not are asking a country to pay for its own good opinion of itself, which is a poorer bargain than either side of the argument usually admits.
paragraphs.label: H
